rationale: A wins because it knows where the floor is: it treats "The carts that skip checkout could be feeding the ad engine that just crossed $1 billion" as a reporting question and says the data link is "not pitchable at all" without confirmation. B has usable bones, but "The $1B threshold is a widely recognized milestone in the retail media category" and "grow across 1,500+ banner partners" smuggle in facts the update did not give. That is the difference between a disciplined angle set and one that starts decorating the empty spots.
gaps_in_A: "The carts that skip checkout could be feeding the ad engine that just crossed $1 billion" is useful as a reporting question, not a pitch; the set admits "nothing in the facts confirms smart-cart data feeds ad targeting," so this needs quarantine until confirmed.

"More grocery chains are letting Instacart's smart carts run their checkout line" overstates the role; the facts say carts skip the checkout line and are expanding, not that Instacart runs a chain's checkout operation.
"Instacart's smart-cart rollout turns it into checkout infrastructure" sits close to the prior grocery-ops angle; it needs commercial terms or an adoption split to be truly separate.
"delivery growth is stalling" is stronger than "slowed to single digits"; get the exact percentage before making that the spine.
gaps_in_B: "The $1B threshold is a widely recognized milestone in the retail media category" is an invented peg; the update gives a run-rate number, not a category rule.
"a stated plan to grow across 1,500+ banner partners" misreads the facts; Instacart has 1,500 retail banners overall, but the update does not say smart carts are planned across all or most of them.
"as digital attribution has gotten harder" imports a market trend not in the update; useful context if sourced, slop if not.
"$1B in Ad Revenue" is sloppy; the source fact is a $1B annual run rate, not booked annual revenue.
